short: A JSON record that Elasticsearch indexes and retrieves as one unit.
detail: An index identifies each document by its _id. Updating a field creates a new Lucene document version under that logical ID.
design: Model documents around read patterns. Denormalizing related data speeds some reads but makes the application responsible for refreshing duplicated values.

short: An index is a named collection of documents, and its mapping defines how Elasticsearch interprets its fields.
detail: Mappings specify field types and options such as the analyzer. An index is partitioned into primary shards at creation.
design: Version mappings and plan reindexing when changing field types. Keep an authoritative copy of the source data so a new index can be rebuilt.

short: A field analyzed into terms for full-text search.
detail: The mapping chooses an analyzer, which usually produces multiple tokens from one string. A match query normally analyzes input with the field’s search analyzer.
design: Choose text for relevance search. Give the same source string a keyword multi-field when queries also need exact equality or sorting.

short: A field that indexes an entire string as one term.
detail: Without a configured normalizer, indexing and exact lookup preserve case and spaces. The keyword multi-field in this sim uses that default.
design: Use keyword for identifiers, labels and exact filters. Sorting or grouping by an analyzed title would group individual tokens instead of the intended values.

short: A pipeline that turns text into the tokens an index or query uses.
detail: An analyzer contains one tokenizer, optional character filters, and zero or more token filters. Index and query can use different analyzers deliberately.
design: Use the Analyze API on representative product names and queries. Accidental differences in normalization can make a healthy index appear to have missing data.

short: The analysis step that splits one string into ordered tokens.
detail: A tokenizer also tracks token positions and character offsets. Lucene’s standard tokenizer uses Unicode word boundaries. This demo splits into runs of letters and digits.
design: Check boundary behavior on hyphenated SKUs, punctuation, and the languages you support. Boundaries affect both retrieval and highlighting.

short: A step that transforms, removes, or inserts tokens after tokenization.
detail: Lowercasing, stop word removal and stemming are three examples. The result of each step feeds the next step.
design: Order filters intentionally. Lowercasing before stop word removal makes The and the behave consistently.

short: Reducing related word forms to a common searchable stem.
detail: A stemmer may turn running and runs into run. The simulator uses a small explicit table for the example vocabulary.
design: Stemming improves recall for prose but can conflate product names and distinct terms. Protect identifiers with a keyword field or an analyzer exclusion.

short: Common tokens a configured filter removes from the token stream.
detail: An English analyzer may remove words such as the and and. If a match query analyzes to zero tokens, its default behavior is to return no documents.
design: Removing common tokens can reduce index noise, but particles and common words can carry meaning in names or phrases. Verify zero-token inputs in the application.

short: A lookup from each indexed term to the documents that contain it.
detail: Each term has a postings list. Queries combine the lists to find candidate documents without scanning every title string.
design: The index buys fast lookups by doing analysis and storing extra structures at write time. Adding analyzers or fields increases write and storage work.

short: The exact value Elasticsearch looks up in a field’s inverted index.
detail: A term may be a word, a stem, or an entire keyword. It is scoped to the field where it was indexed.
design: Inspect indexed terms when debugging missing hits. The original string in _source may look nothing like the searchable representation.

short: The list of documents containing a particular term.
detail: For analyzed text, postings can store a document ID, term frequency, and token positions. Intersection requires membership in all lists, while union needs any.
design: Query cost depends on the lengths and combinations of postings. Broad terms can expand candidate work even when the response returns only a few hits.

short: How many times a term occurs in a particular document field.
detail: BM25 applies a saturating function to frequency. Increasing a term from once to twice usually matters more than increasing it from ten to eleven.
design: Compare frequency with field length when a repetitive title outranks cleaner copy. Raw occurrence count alone is an incomplete relevance signal.

short: A scoring weight that gives rare terms more influence.
detail: Lucene’s BM25 uses log(1 + (N − df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)). N counts documents with the field, and df counts documents containing the term.
design: An unchanged document can move in rank as the corpus changes. With shard-local statistics, small or skewed shards can also make scores less comparable.

short: The default relevance scoring method for analyzed Elasticsearch text fields.
detail: It combines term rarity, saturating frequency, and field-length normalization. This demo sums Lucene-style unit-boost contributions with k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75.
design: Use score explanations and judged query examples when tuning relevance. A score is relative to the query, field, and search corpus.

short: A scoring adjustment based on a field’s token count relative to its average.
detail: For the same term frequency, a longer field increases the BM25 denominator. The demo uses exact token counts instead of Lucene’s compact stored norms.
design: Compare titles with titles and descriptions with descriptions. Combining both into one field can make useful matches behave differently than you expect.

short: A query that analyzes input before looking up terms in an analyzed field.
detail: With multiple terms, the default operator is OR. Set operator to AND to require every analyzed term. Adjacent words need a phrase query when exact order matters.
design: Start with match for user-entered search text. Test recall before tightening the operator, especially when users type adjectives or alternate spellings.

short: A query that looks up one value without the text analysis pipeline.
detail: Running shoes is one literal lookup, while analyzed text usually indexes separate terms. Looking up the actual indexed term run can match a text field.
design: Use term queries for exact IDs and keyword values. A term query sent to the wrong mapping can return zero hits with a successful response.

short: Combines query clauses using required, optional, excluded, or filter semantics.
detail: In this demo, AND requires every analyzed term and intersects postings. OR allows any term and unions postings.
design: Use boolean structure to separate hard filters, such as tenant authorization, from score-producing optional clauses that improve ranking.

short: Memory holding writes that Lucene has yet to publish to search.
detail: A refresh can write buffered data into a new segment and open it for search. The translog separately records operations for crash recovery.
design: Size concurrent indexing to avoid excessive memory pressure. More frequent refreshes can reduce the amount of data amortized across each segment.

short: An immutable piece of a shard’s index.
detail: A segment stores its own term dictionary and postings. Deletions are tracked outside the immutable indexed content, and merges rewrite that content into new segments.
design: Many small segments raise search and merge overhead. Batch ingestion and choose refresh settings that match your freshness target.

short: Publishes recent operations to a new search view.
detail: Lucene can open newly written segments and apply delete markers without a durable Lucene commit. A refresh with only deletes can change visibility without adding indexed documents.
design: Use refresh=wait_for when search must see a just-written change. Forcing refresh on individual writes can generate many tiny segments.

short: The configured cadence for automatic search visibility.
detail: Elastic Stack normally refreshes a searched index about once per second. Default search-idle behavior and Serverless settings can differ. Setting refresh_interval to -1 disables periodic refresh.
design: Treat search freshness as a budget. A longer interval batches indexing work while letting readers observe older data for longer.

short: Search observes write changes after a short refresh delay.
detail: An acknowledged index request does not itself refresh the search reader. A real-time GET by ID is a separate read path.
design: Define what the user should see immediately after a write. Showing their saved record from the write response can avoid forcing a refresh for every search.

short: The operation log Lucene shard recovery can replay after its last durable commit.
detail: Index, update, and delete operations enter a translog. Request durability syncs it before acknowledgement. Async durability syncs it on a timer and can lose unsynced writes.
design: Budget for replay time as well as write throughput. With async durability, decide how the source system will detect and repair acknowledged writes lost in a crash.

short: A request to persist pending file changes to durable storage.
detail: Request durability coordinates a translog fsync on the primary and allocated replicas before success. With async durability the regular default sync interval is five seconds.
design: Batching can amortize disk barriers, but asynchronous acknowledgement gives up some durability. Measure the write latency cost against the loss window the product can tolerate.

short: Commits Lucene index state to durable storage and rolls the translog generation.
detail: After the commit, operations it contains no longer need replay from the old translog. Elasticsearch normally flushes automatically as needed.
design: Flush controls the recovery checkpoint and replay size. Use refresh controls when the requirement is immediate search visibility.

short: Rewrites older segments into fewer segments and can reclaim eligible deleted versions.
detail: Search keeps using its existing view while a merge builds output. Merge policy decides which segments to combine and which retained records must survive.
design: Budget I/O and temporary disk headroom for merges. Forcing large merges on a live write-heavy index can make throughput and latency worse.

short: A marker that hides a deleted or superseded document version.
detail: An update indexes a replacement and marks the earlier version deleted. Search stops returning the old version after refresh. Eligible dead data can be reclaimed at merge.
design: Expect churn-heavy workloads to consume more disk than the live document size suggests. Retention leases can keep operation history for replica recovery.

short: A partition of an Elasticsearch index, backed by a Lucene index.
detail: Each shard has one primary and can have replica copies. Full-index search runs against one active copy of each requested shard.
design: Shard count governs placement, recovery units, and full-query fan-out. Size shards from measured data volume, indexing, and search load.

short: The authoritative copy of a shard that accepts and sequences writes.
detail: An index’s primary count is fixed for its current layout. A new index, reindex, split, or shrink can produce a different layout. An in-sync replica can take over as primary.
design: Estimate how data and write traffic distribute across primaries before creation. Adding replicas increases copies and read capacity, while write routing still follows the primaries.

short: A copy of one primary shard on a different node.
detail: Replicas handle reads and an in-sync replica can be promoted after primary failure. Recovery creates a new ready replica by copying missing shard data.
design: Place replicas across failure domains where possible. Their storage and write replication costs buy higher availability and additional search capacity.

short: A hash of the routing key decides which primary receives a document.
detail: Document ID is the usual key. A shared tenant key sends the tenant’s writes to one shard in the ordinary unpartitioned layout. Older index versions can use a routing-shard factor.
design: Tenant routing can reduce targeted search fan-out at the cost of hotspot risk. Check tenant skew and carry the same key through reads, updates, and deletes.

short: The node that receives a search request and combines the shard responses.
detail: It dispatches query work to one copy per requested shard, merges the returned candidates, and fetches the winning documents.
design: Count the coordinator’s heap and network budget separately from shard work. Large result windows and wide fan-out can overload a coordinator while data nodes look healthy.

short: Search first collects ranked candidates, then retrieves the winning documents.
detail: Shard copies send IDs with scores or sort values in the query phase. The coordinator chooses the global page and requests its document bodies during the fetch phase.
design: Returning five documents can still require a large distributed top-K. Inspect query and fetch costs separately when debugging latency.

short: Fetching late pages by specifying a large offset.
detail: Each shard can collect up to from + size candidates, since it cannot know how many earlier hits other shards contain. The coordinator merges and discards the prefix.
design: Cap arbitrary offsets in public APIs. Use a cursor for browsing and avoid turning a small response into large cross-shard sort and heap work.

short: A cursor based on the last result’s sort values.
detail: On the next request, shards collect competitive hits after the supplied sort values. A stable tie-breaker keeps ordering unambiguous. A point in time keeps the view consistent across refreshes.
design: Use it for sequential browsing past the result window. Cursor pagination limits candidate state, while the query may still need to evaluate many matching documents.

short: A summary of whether configured primary and replica copies are assigned.
detail: Green means all copies are assigned. Yellow means all primaries are assigned but replicas are missing. Red means at least one primary is missing.
design: Alert on yellow for lost redundancy. At red, inspect per-shard failures and decide whether clients can use partial results for the request they made.

short: Choosing a shard count that balances fan-out with placement and recovery.
detail: Oversharding leaves many small shards whose fixed costs can dominate. Too few shards can create large recovery units, limited placement, or hot primaries.
design: Test shard sizing at actual query and ingestion rates. Include node failure and the time required to rebuild replicas when comparing layouts.

short: A distributed count of common values, built by combining each shard’s leading buckets.
detail: shard_size controls how many candidate buckets a shard sends. For the default descending count order, reported doc_count_error_upper_bound bounds possible missing counts.
design: Raising shard_size can improve top-bucket accuracy at a network and heap cost. Consider composite aggregation for deterministic enumeration of all buckets.
